Key protections: 2-year statutory guarantee for goods, right to repair before replacement, 14-day cooling-off period for distance contracts, rules on free-to-consumer digital services (social media) treating personal data as the 'price.' The CCPC enforces consumer law. Package holiday regulations (2018) protect holidaymakers. Unfair contract terms in standard consumer contracts are automatically void. The National Consumer Agency merger into CCPC brought consumer and competition enforcement together.
laws.penalty: Unfair commercial practices: CCPC enforcement, prohibition orders, fines. Consumer contract breaches: civil remedies including repair, replacement, refund.
exceptions: B2B contracts have more limited protections (commercial parties assumed equal bargaining power)
Second-hand goods sold at auction between consumers have reduced statutory guarantee

quiz.q: What is the statutory guarantee period for goods purchased under Ireland's Consumer Rights Act 2022?
quiz.explanation: Under Ireland's Consumer Rights Act 2022 (implementing EU directives), consumers have a 2-year statutory guarantee for goods, during which sellers must repair, replace, or refund faulty products. The first 12 months have a reversed burden of proof—the seller must prove the product was not faulty.

laws.title: Overseas Development Aid
laws.subtitle: Irish Aid and International Development Policy
laws.fullDescription: Ireland has strong tradition of international development aid, partly rooted in memory of the Famine. Irish Aid (Department of Foreign Affairs) manages approximately €850 million annually in Official Development Assistance (ODA). Ireland has been a strong supporter of UNHCR, WFP, and UNICEF. The 0.7% of GNI target for development aid has been missed; Ireland's ODA/GNI ratio is approximately 0.3-0.4%. Irish missionaries and NGOs (Concern, GOAL, Trócaire) have long histories in humanitarian work. The 2021 Global Ireland strategy promotes Irish development leadership.
laws.penalty: No domestic criminal penalties; international accountability through OECD DAC peer review processes.
exceptions: Emergency humanitarian aid can be deployed faster than development programs
NGO funding requires compliance with Irish Aid standards and anti-money laundering rules

quiz.q: Approximately how much does Ireland spend annually on Official Development Assistance?
quiz.explanation: Ireland spends approximately €850 million annually on Official Development Assistance (ODA) through Irish Aid, focusing on sub-Saharan Africa and emergency humanitarian response. Despite this, Ireland has not yet met the international 0.7% of GNI target.

laws.title: Domestic Violence Law
laws.subtitle: Domestic Violence Act 2018
laws.fullDescription: The 2018 Domestic Violence Act consolidated and updated Irish domestic violence law. Safety orders and barring orders protect victims from abusers. Emergency barring orders (up to 8 working days) can be obtained ex parte (without the abuser present). The offense of coercive control was created—recognizing patterns of behavior rather than requiring physical violence. Domestic violence is now treated as an aggravating factor in related criminal offenses. Refuge places remain critically insufficient: Ireland has one of the lowest rates of refuge accommodation in Europe. Safe Ireland coordinates the domestic violence sector.
laws.penalty: Breach of safety/barring order: up to 12 months imprisonment. Coercive control: up to 10 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Safety orders can be sought by those in intimate relationships without living together
Children can be named in barring orders for their protection

quiz.q: What new offense criminalizing patterns of controlling behavior was created in Ireland's 2018 Domestic Violence Act?
quiz.explanation: The Domestic Violence Act 2018 created the offense of coercive control, recognizing that domestic abuse often involves patterns of controlling behavior—financial control, isolation, monitoring, threats—rather than just physical violence. The offense carries up to 10 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Aviation Law and Dublin Airport
laws.subtitle: Air Navigation and Transport Acts
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's strategic location makes it a major aviation hub. Dublin Airport is Ireland's main international gateway (33+ million passengers in 2023). The DAA (Dublin Airport Authority) operates Dublin and Cork airports. Aer Lingus (owned by IAG) and Ryanair (Europe's largest low-cost carrier, headquartered in Dublin) dominate Irish aviation. The controversy over a planned second Dublin Airport terminal and capacity cap (32 million passengers) has limited expansion. Irish air traffic control (IAA) was split into two bodies in 2022 (safety regulation and service provision). Open Skies agreement with the US enables transatlantic connections.
laws.penalty: Aviation safety violations: IAA enforcement, certificate revocation, fines. Unlicensed air operations: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: State aircraft (military, police) have exemptions from commercial air law
Aircraft in distress may violate airspace rules without penalty

quiz.q: What is the ownership structure of Aer Lingus, Ireland's flag carrier airline?
options: Independently listed on Irish Stock Exchange
quiz.explanation: Aer Lingus is owned by IAG (International Airlines Group), the parent company of British Airways and Iberia, which acquired it in 2015. Despite Irish government shareholding sold, the airline is contractually obligated to maintain its Dublin hub and transatlantic routes.

laws.title: Healthcare Rights and Right to Life
laws.subtitle: Constitution Article 40.3.3 and Health Acts
laws.fullDescription: The right to life is protected in Article 40.3 of the Irish Constitution, which was the basis of the Eighth Amendment (1983-2018) equating unborn and mother's right to life. The 2018 repeal referendum fundamentally changed this framework. The Irish courts developed 'right to die' jurisprudence in the Marie Fleming case (2013)—Supreme Court held no right to assisted suicide but the Oireachtas may legislate. A 2024 Citizens' Assembly on End of Life Care recommended allowing assisted dying in limited circumstances. Legislation is pending. The right to healthcare is not explicit in the constitution but is derived from personal rights.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed medical practice: criminal prosecution. Right to life violations by state: constitutional damages.
exceptions: Right to refuse medical treatment (autonomy) is established under Irish law
Advance Care Directives Act 2015 permits binding refusal of treatment

quiz.q: What did Ireland's 2024 Citizens' Assembly on End of Life Care recommend?
options: Allowing assisted dying in limited circumstances
Complete ban on all assisted dying discussion
Mandatory palliative care for all terminal patients
Referendum on constitutional right to healthcare
quiz.explanation: Ireland's 2024 Citizens' Assembly on End of Life Care recommended allowing assisted dying in limited circumstances, a significant shift that could lead to legislation similar to jurisdictions like Belgium, Canada, or parts of Australia.

laws.title: Witness Protection Programme
laws.subtitle: Criminal Justice Act 1999
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's witness protection program is relatively small and underfunded compared to US or UK equivalents. The Program provides security, relocated identity, and financial support for witnesses to serious organized crime. Garda National Bureau of Criminal Investigation (GNBCI) manages it. Its existence in law was only formally acknowledged in recent years—previously officially unconfirmed. The Kinahan-Hutch feud created significant witness intimidation challenges. The Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017 provides broader victim rights including information, protection, and participation in proceedings.
laws.penalty: Witness intimidation: up to 10 years imprisonment. Perverting the course of justice: up to life imprisonment in extreme cases.
exceptions: Witness can withdraw from programme voluntarily
Legal professional privilege still applies for legal advisors to witnesses

quiz.q: What Irish legislation formally provided rights for crime victims including information and protection?
quiz.explanation: The Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act 2017 transposed the EU Victims' Rights Directive and formally established victim rights in Ireland, including rights to information about their case, protection from the accused, interpretation and translation, and participation in criminal proceedings.

laws.title: Special Education Law
laws.subtitle: Education for Persons with Special Educational Needs (EPSEN) Act 2004
laws.fullDescription: The EPSEN Act 2004 established the right of children with special educational needs (SEN) to be educated in an inclusive school environment where possible. The National Council for Special Education (NCSE) allocates Special Education Teachers and Special Needs Assistants (SNAs). Ireland has approximately 20,000 SNAs—one of the highest rates in the world. ASD (autism spectrum disorder) units in mainstream schools have expanded but demand exceeds supply. Parents have the right to appeal NCSE decisions. The Disability Act 2005 added assessment of need provisions. Educational psychologist wait times are a systemic problem.
laws.penalty: Schools refusing reasonable accommodations for students with disabilities: equality complaints, EPSEN enforcement.
exceptions: Full EPSEN provisions have only been partially commenced—individual education plans not universally mandated
Private schools have some flexibility in SEN admissions

quiz.q: Approximately how many Special Needs Assistants (SNAs) does Ireland employ in schools?
quiz.explanation: Ireland employs approximately 20,000 Special Needs Assistants (SNAs) in schools, one of the highest rates per capita in the world, reflecting significant investment in supported inclusion of students with disabilities and special educational needs in mainstream education.

laws.title: Agricultural Support and CAP
laws.subtitle: Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Implementation
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's agriculture sector receives approximately €1.8 billion annually from the EU Common Agricultural Policy. The 2023-2027 CAP Strategic Plan for Ireland emphasizes eco-schemes rewarding farmers for environmental practices. Beef and dairy are the dominant sectors. The 2023 fertilizer levy added costs for farmers. Teagasc (Agriculture and Food Development Authority) provides research, advisory, and training. Bord Bia promotes Irish food exports (€17 billion in 2023). The Nitrates Action Programme and water quality obligations create compliance requirements for farmers.
laws.penalty: CAP subsidy fraud: repayment plus penalties, exclusion from future payments. Environmental compliance violations: subsidy reduction (cross-compliance).
exceptions: Organic farmers qualify for enhanced payments under CAP eco-schemes
Young farmer top-ups encourage generational renewal in farming
laws.sourceLabel: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine

quiz.q: Approximately how much does Ireland's agriculture sector receive annually from EU CAP payments?
quiz.explanation: Ireland's agriculture sector receives approximately €1.8 billion annually from the EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), supporting beef, dairy, sheep, and tillage farmers through direct payments, rural development funding, and market support measures.

laws.title: Prison Law and Penal Policy
laws.subtitle: Prisons Act 2007
laws.fullDescription: The Irish Prison Service manages 14 prisons with a certified capacity of approximately 4,000 but chronic overcrowding (actual population often 4,200+). Mountjoy Prison (Dublin) is the most notorious—built in 1850 Victorian design. The Inspector of Prisons reports on conditions. Ireland has one of the lowest prisoner rates in the EU (approximately 80 per 100,000). The 2007 Prisons Act modernized prison rules. Open prisons (Loughan House) and community return programs reduce recidivism. The Irish Penal Reform Trust advocates for reforms. Solitary confinement (designated cells) faces human rights challenges.
laws.penalty: Prisoners retain civil rights except those necessarily forfeited by imprisonment. Misconduct within prison: additional days, restricted regime.
exceptions: Temporary release (parole) is executive decision not automatic
Prisoners serving life sentences require Parole Board recommendation for release

quiz.q: Approximately what is Ireland's prisoner rate per 100,000 people?
quiz.explanation: Ireland has one of the lowest imprisonment rates in the EU at approximately 80 prisoners per 100,000 population, compared to EU averages of around 130 and the US rate of over 600 per 100,000, reflecting a relatively lower emphasis on custodial sentences.

laws.title: Social Housing Scheme
laws.subtitle: Housing Acts and Social Housing Assessment
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's social housing waiting list peaked at approximately 91,000 households in 2016 and stood at approximately 57,000 in 2023 following significant build output. Local authorities and Approved Housing Bodies (AHBs) provide social housing. The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) scheme—where tenants find private rented accommodation and HAP subsidizes it—has been criticized for propping up private rents and offering insecure tenure. Rebuilding Ireland (2016-2021) and Housing for All (2022+) are successive government plans. Rent supplement and Housing Assistance Payment support about 200,000 households in private rental.
laws.penalty: HAP fraud (false declarations of income): repayment and potential prosecution. Illegal subletting of social housing: termination of tenancy.
exceptions: Emergency social housing for those in domestic violence situations has expedited pathway
Priority for homeless households on social housing lists

quiz.q: What Irish housing scheme allows tenants to find private rented accommodation with state subsidizing the rent?
quiz.explanation: The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) scheme allows qualifying social housing applicants to find their own private rented accommodation while the state (via local authorities) pays most of the rent directly to landlords. Critics argue HAP keeps tenants in insecure private rental rather than providing permanent social housing.

laws.title: Territory and Neutrality
laws.subtitle: Irish Defence Acts and Neutrality Policy
laws.fullDescription: Ireland maintains a policy of military neutrality—not a member of NATO, no military alliances, no foreign military bases permitted. The 'triple lock' requires UN mandate, Government approval, and Dáil approval for overseas military deployments. Ireland participates in EU PESCO (Permanent Structured Cooperation) and Partnership for Peace (NATO) without full NATO membership. Shannon Airport's use by US military has been controversial—the government allows US military overflights and stops without searching aircraft (relying on diplomatic assurances). Ireland deployed to UN peacekeeping missions in Lebanon (UNIFIL), Syria, and elsewhere.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized foreign military presence: expulsion under international law. Shannon activism (protesters have attempted to inspect US planes): prosecuted under criminal damage and trespass laws.
exceptions: PESCO participation allows EU defense cooperation without undermining formal neutrality
UN peacekeeping missions authorized by triple lock

quiz.q: What is Ireland's 'triple lock' requirement for overseas military deployments?
options: UN mandate + Government approval + Dáil approval
NATO authorization + EU approval + Government approval
Security Council + EU Council + Irish Cabinet approval
quiz.explanation: Ireland's 'triple lock' requires three conditions for overseas military deployment: a UN Security Council or UN General Assembly mandate, Irish government (Cabinet) approval, and Dáil (parliament) approval. This mechanism was designed to ensure Ireland's military neutrality is maintained and deployments only occur through legitimate multilateral channels.

laws.title: Tourism and Cultural Heritage Law
laws.subtitle: National Monuments Acts and Tourism Acts
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's tourism sector (10+ million visitors pre-COVID, recovering to similar levels by 2023) is supported by Fáilte Ireland (domestic/inbound tourism) and Tourism Ireland (island of Ireland promotion). The National Monuments Act protects archaeological heritage. The 2023 Heritage Bill expanded protections for vernacular architecture. Skellig Michael (UNESCO World Heritage Site) faces visitor pressure. Tax relief for heritage buildings (Section 482) incentivizes restoration. The Wild Atlantic Way and Ireland's Ancient East are major tourism brands. Short-term letting platforms face planning restrictions in tourist areas that are damaging rental supply.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized excavation of archaeological site: up to 5 years imprisonment. Damage to national monument: criminal prosecution and restoration orders.
exceptions: Agricultural activities on undesignated archaeological sites may continue with notification
Planning permission may allow development with archaeological mitigation

quiz.q: What UNESCO World Heritage Site off the Kerry coast faces pressure from tourism visitor numbers?
quiz.explanation: Skellig Michael, a remote rocky island off the Kerry coast that served as a monastic settlement (and more recently as a Star Wars filming location), is a UNESCO World Heritage Site facing significant visitor management challenges due to its popularity and the fragility of its ancient stone structures.

laws.title: Homicide Law
laws.subtitle: Criminal Justice Act 1964
laws.fullDescription: Murder in Ireland requires malice aforethought (intent to kill or cause serious injury, or knowledge that death was likely consequence). Mandatory life sentence for murder (minimum 40 years tariff for killing a Garda or prison officer). Manslaughter (unlawful killing without malice) carries maximum life imprisonment. Provocation is a partial defense (now 'loss of self-control' following 2023 reforms). Infanticide is a specific lesser offense for mothers. Ireland has no death penalty (abolished 1990, constitutionally prohibited since 2001). The Law Reform Commission recommended significant homicide law reform in 2023.
laws.penalty: Murder: mandatory life imprisonment (no parole for first 12-40 years depending on victim). Manslaughter: up to life imprisonment.
exceptions: Diminished responsibility may reduce murder to manslaughter
Self-defense (lawful use of force in defense of person or dwelling) is a complete defense

quiz.q: What is the minimum tariff before parole consideration for murder of a Garda (police officer) in Ireland?
quiz.explanation: The murder of a Garda (police officer) or prison officer in Ireland carries an enhanced minimum tariff of 40 years before parole eligibility can be considered. This reflects the aggravated nature of killing those serving in protective roles in the justice system.

laws.title: Fisheries and Marine Resources
laws.subtitle: Sea Fisheries and Maritime Jurisdiction Act 2006
laws.fullDescription: Ireland has significant fishing rights in its large EEZ (220 million acres). The Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (SFPA) enforces conservation rules. Post-Brexit, the Trade and Cooperation Agreement allocated catches between the UK, EU, and Ireland—causing significant controversy for Irish fishers who had fished in UK waters. The Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) sets total allowable catches. Fishing communities in the west and southwest face economic pressure. Aquaculture (salmon, shellfish) faces planning and environmental regulation. Illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing is a significant enforcement challenge.
laws.penalty: Overfishing quotas: fines, vessel decommissioning, loss of fishing licenses. IUU fishing: up to €100,000 fine.
exceptions: Small inshore fishing vessels have simplified licensing under 10-meter rules
Traditional coastal fishing communities have some historical access protections

quiz.q: What post-Brexit agreement affected Irish fishing rights in UK waters?
quiz.explanation: The UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) signed in December 2020 reallocated fishing rights in UK and EU waters, reducing Irish and EU fishing access to UK waters by approximately 25% over 5 years, causing significant controversy and financial impact for Irish fishing communities.

laws.title: Fintech and Digital Banking
laws.subtitle: Payment Services Regulations 2018 (PSD2) and Electronic Money Regulations
laws.fullDescription: Ireland is a major hub for fintech—Stripe, Square, Adyen, Revolut (regulated by Central Bank), and PayPal have Ireland operations. The Payment Services Regulations 2018 (implementing EU PSD2) enable open banking: banks must allow licensed third parties to access account data with customer consent. The Central Bank regulates e-money institutions (Revolut's EU license is Irish) and payment institutions. Buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) regulation has been introduced following EU Consumer Credit Directive amendments. Cryptocurrency exchanges must register with the Central Bank for anti-money laundering compliance.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed payment services: fines up to €500,000. AML non-compliance: up to 5 years imprisonment and unlimited fines.
exceptions: Limited networks and intracompany payment systems have reduced requirements
Pre-2009 legacy payment systems grandfathered under simplified rules

quiz.q: Which major fintech company holds its EU banking license from the Irish Central Bank?
quiz.explanation: Revolut, the UK-founded digital banking app, obtained its EU banking license from the Irish Central Bank, making Ireland its EU regulatory home. This allows Revolut to operate banking services across the EU market through the Irish license.

laws.title: Child and Family Agency (Tusla)
laws.subtitle: Child and Family Agency Act 2013
laws.fullDescription: Tusla (Child and Family Agency) was established in 2013, separated from HSE, to focus exclusively on child protection, family support, and adoption. Ireland has approximately 5,500 children in care—either foster care (preferred) or residential care. The 2019 Review of Tusla found systemic understaffing and poor case management for the most vulnerable children. Mandatory reporting of suspected child abuse by professionals (teachers, doctors, social workers) is required under the 2015 Children First Act. An Garda Síochána and Tusla jointly investigate abuse allegations. Adoption is regulated under the Adoption Act 2010.
laws.penalty: Failure to report child abuse by mandated reporters: criminal prosecution under Children First Act.
exceptions: Legal professional privilege may limit disclosure in some circumstances
Reasonable belief standard applies—reporters need not be certain abuse occurred

quiz.q: What legislation made reporting of suspected child abuse mandatory for professionals in Ireland?
quiz.explanation: The Children First Act 2015 placed mandatory reporting obligations on a wide range of professionals (teachers, doctors, nurses, social workers, Gardaí, and others) to report suspected child abuse or neglect to Tusla. Failure to report is a criminal offense.

laws.title: Air Quality Law
laws.subtitle: Air Pollution Acts 1987-2011
laws.fullDescription: Ireland banned smoky coal in Dublin (1990) and expanded the ban nationally (2022)—dramatically improving urban air quality. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) enforces air quality standards under EU directives. Wood burning stoves face new restrictions on moisture content since 2022. Peat harvesting by Bord na Móna and private operators has been phased out for energy use (Edenderry power station converted to biomass). Mobile emissions testing for vehicles. The Leinster ban on bituminous coal reduced Dublins' winter smog significantly. Ireland's air quality is generally good by EU standards except during temperature inversions.
laws.penalty: Burning prohibited fuels (smoky coal): fines up to €5,000. Industrial air emissions violations: EPA enforcement, fines up to €15 million.
exceptions: Rural areas with no alternative heating in extreme weather may have enforcement discretion
Agricultural burning within strict seasonal windows with advance notice

quiz.q: When did Ireland ban smoky (bituminous) coal in Dublin, dramatically improving air quality?
quiz.explanation: Dublin's smoky coal ban was introduced in 1990, significantly reducing winter air pollution. The ban was gradually extended nationwide, with a complete national ban on smoky coal sales and distribution taking effect in 2022, significantly improving air quality across Ireland.

laws.title: Artificial Intelligence Policy
laws.subtitle: EU AI Act Implementation (2024)
laws.fullDescription: Ireland will be a key implementing state for the EU AI Act (2024), which became law in August 2024 with phased implementation. As home to major AI developers (Google DeepMind Dublin, Meta AI, Microsoft Azure AI), Ireland's regulatory approach is globally significant. The Central Bank, DPC, and Coimisiún na Meán will be relevant national authorities for AI in their sectors. The AI Act prohibits unacceptable risk AI (social scoring, real-time biometrics in public), heavily regulates high-risk AI (medical, employment, justice), and has lighter rules for low-risk. Ireland has invested in AI Ireland research cluster.
laws.penalty: EU AI Act violations for prohibited AI practices: up to €35 million or 7% of global turnover. High-risk AI violations: up to €15 million or 3% of turnover.
exceptions: Military and national security AI falls outside EU AI Act
Research and development AI in testing environments has reduced obligations

quiz.q: What category of AI does the EU AI Act completely prohibit?
options: Unacceptable risk AI (social scoring, real-time public biometrics)
quiz.explanation: The EU AI Act prohibits 'unacceptable risk' AI systems including social scoring by governments, most real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces, AI that exploits vulnerabilities, and subliminal manipulation. These prohibitions apply in all EU member states including Ireland.

laws.title: Fraud and White Collar Crime
laws.subtitle: Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act 2001
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's 2001 Theft and Fraud Act consolidated theft, fraud, and deception offenses. Major white collar crime cases have included the Anglo Irish Bank prosecutions, Revenue evasion by prominent businesspeople (Ben Dunne), and insurance fraud rings. The Garda National Economic Crime Bureau (GNECB) investigates major fraud. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission investigates cartels. Director of Corporate Enforcement (ODCE, now Corporate Enforcement Authority) prosecutes company law violations. The 2023 CEA Act strengthened investigation powers. Ireland's financial crisis produced some of the most expensive banking prosecutions in European history.
laws.penalty: Theft: up to 10 years imprisonment. Fraud: up to 10 years. Making gain by deception: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Civil recovery through courts as alternative/addition to criminal prosecution
Statute of limitations for some fraud offenses extended to accommodate complex investigations

quiz.q: What body investigates major fraud in Ireland?
quiz.explanation: The Garda National Economic Crime Bureau (GNECB) is Ireland's specialist policing unit for investigating major fraud, money laundering, cybercrime with financial dimensions, and complex economic crime, working alongside the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission and Corporate Enforcement Authority.

laws.title: Mental Health Services and Crisis Care
laws.subtitle: Mental Health Act 2001 and National Mental Health Policy
laws.fullDescription: A Vision for Change (2006-2016) and Sharing the Vision (2020-2024) are Ireland's successive national mental health policy frameworks. The HSE mental health services employ approximately 10,000 staff but face chronic underfunding (mental health receives about 6.5% of overall health budget versus WHO recommended 10-12%). Waiting lists for child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) scandal emerged in 2021: children languishing on waiting lists for years. The Maskey Report (2022) found significant failings in CAMHS West. Samaritans Ireland, Pieta House, and SpunOut provide crisis support. 24-hour crisis text lines were expanded.
laws.penalty: No direct penalties; mental health service failures addressed through HSE accountability, Oireachtas scrutiny, and media pressure.
exceptions: Emergency mental health assessment at A&E available without referral
Community mental health teams provide outreach to those unable to attend clinics

quiz.q: What percentage of Ireland's overall health budget is allocated to mental health services?
quiz.explanation: Ireland allocates approximately 6.5% of its overall health budget to mental health services, below the WHO's recommended 10-12% minimum, contributing to long waiting lists and service gaps particularly in child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS).

laws.title: Energy Market Regulation
laws.subtitle: Electricity Regulation Act 1999 and Gas Acts
laws.fullDescription: The Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU) regulates electricity and gas markets in Ireland. EirGrid manages the national electricity grid; Gas Networks Ireland operates the gas distribution system. The all-island Single Electricity Market (SEM) with Northern Ireland creates a unique cross-border energy market (unique post-Brexit arrangement). Electricity prices have been among the EU's highest, partly due to high renewable integration and grid costs. The 2022-2023 energy crisis prompted government emergency credits (€600 per household). LNG import terminal proposals face environmental opposition.
laws.penalty: Price gouging during energy crisis: CCPC investigation and enforcement. Market manipulation: CRU sanctions.
exceptions: Public service obligation (PSO) levy funds renewable energy and peat transition
Energy poverty protections limit disconnection of vulnerable customers

quiz.q: What unique cross-border energy market arrangement exists between Ireland and Northern Ireland?
quiz.explanation: The Single Electricity Market (SEM) is a unique all-island electricity market covering both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, maintained even after Brexit through special arrangements in the Northern Ireland Protocol/Windsor Framework, allowing continued cross-border electricity trading.

laws.title: Emergency Powers and Civil Contingencies
laws.subtitle: Emergency Powers Act 1939 and Health Act 2020 (COVID provisions)
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's emergency powers have been invoked rarely—most recently for COVID-19. The Health (Preservation and Protection and Other Emergency Measures in the Public Interest) Act 2020 gave government extraordinary powers to restrict movement ('Level 5 lockdown'), close businesses, and mandate public health measures. Ireland had some of Europe's longest and strictest lockdowns (March 2020-May 2021). The legislation sunset after the emergency. Courts largely upheld restrictions as proportionate constitutional limitations during genuine emergency. Post-COVID review recommended formal civil contingencies legislation.
laws.penalty: Lockdown breaches: fixed charge notices €100-500. Garda could arrest non-compliant persons. Businesses violating closure orders: prosecution.
exceptions: Essential workers exempted from movement restrictions
Emergency services and healthcare workers had different rules

quiz.q: Approximately how long were Ireland's COVID-19 lockdown restrictions in place?
quiz.explanation: Ireland maintained COVID-19 restrictions from March 2020 until approximately May 2021, over 14 months, making it one of Europe's longest and most stringent lockdown regimes. Ireland went through multiple 'Level 5' full lockdowns and various intermediate restriction levels during this period.

laws.title: EU Law Supremacy in Ireland
laws.subtitle: European Communities Act 1972 and EU Treaties
laws.fullDescription: Ireland joined the EEC in 1973 and has been a deeply integrated EU member. EU law takes supremacy over Irish domestic law under the Crotty doctrine (1987)—the Supreme Court ruled that significant EU treaty changes require Irish constitutional amendment and hence referendum. Ireland has voted on EU treaties in referendums: ratified Lisbon Treaty only after second referendum (2009, first rejected 2008). The Single Market and EU regulations directly apply in Ireland. European Court of Justice (ECJ) rulings bind Ireland. Brexit has greatly elevated Ireland's strategic importance within the EU.
laws.penalty: EU law violations by Ireland: European Commission infringement proceedings, ECJ fines, Court judgments overriding Irish law.
exceptions: Subsidiarity principle preserves national competence in areas not EU-competence
National implementation choices for directives within permitted margins

quiz.q: What is the Crotty doctrine in Irish constitutional law?
options: Significant EU treaty changes require Irish referendum approval
EU law has absolute supremacy over the Irish constitution
Ireland can opt out of any EU regulation
EU officials are immune from Irish criminal prosecution
quiz.explanation: The Crotty doctrine, established by the Irish Supreme Court in 1987, holds that significant changes to EU treaties that fundamentally alter Ireland's constitutional position require a referendum to amend the Irish constitution, not just Oireachtas approval—a uniquely Irish requirement that has led to multiple EU treaty referendums.

laws.title: Money Laundering Law
laws.subtitle: Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Acts 2010-2021
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's AML/CFT framework implements EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives (6AMLD as of 2022). The Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU Ireland) at An Garda Síochána receives suspicious transaction reports (STRs) from banks, accountants, lawyers, and estate agents. Ireland has been identified by the FATF as generally compliant but with enforcement gaps. The Criminal Assets Bureau targets proceeds of crime without needing criminal conviction. Ireland is a major hub for financial flows—Shell companies and trust structures have been misused. The 2023 Companies (Corporate Enforcement Authority) Act strengthened enforcement.
laws.penalty: Money laundering: up to 14 years imprisonment. Terrorist financing: up to 14 years. Failure to report suspicious transactions: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Legal professional privilege for lawyers receiving information in criminal defense context
De minimis transactions below reporting thresholds have reduced obligations

quiz.q: What Irish body receives suspicious transaction reports from banks and financial institutions?
options: Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU Ireland) at An Garda Síochána
quiz.explanation: FIU Ireland, based within An Garda Síochána (Irish police), is Ireland's Financial Intelligence Unit responsible for receiving, analyzing, and disseminating suspicious transaction reports (STRs) from banks, accountants, lawyers, and other regulated entities to detect money laundering and terrorist financing.

laws.title: Sports Law and Governance
laws.subtitle: Sport Ireland Act 2015
laws.fullDescription: Sport Ireland (formerly the Irish Sports Council) funds and governs sport in Ireland. Unique to Ireland: the GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association) is the world's largest amateur sporting organization by participation, operating county and club structure with no professional league—though this is evolving with player payments debates. FAI (Football Association of Ireland) governance scandal (John Delaney era, 2019) required Sport Ireland to withhold funding pending governance reforms. Horse Racing Ireland and Horse Sport Ireland are separate bodies with major economic impact. Doping control follows WADA code; Sport Ireland Institute provides elite athlete support.
laws.penalty: Match-fixing: Criminal Justice (Corruption Offences) Act penalties up to 10 years. Doping: competition ban per WADA code.
exceptions: Amateur sports clubs below Sport Ireland funding threshold have reduced governance requirements
Traditional GAA county structures have significant autonomy from Sport Ireland oversight

quiz.q: What scandal involving the Football Association of Ireland in 2019 led to funding being withheld?
options: Doping revelations by Irish soccer team
Match-fixing by Irish Premier Division clubs
quiz.explanation: The FAI (Football Association of Ireland) governance scandal centered on CEO John Delaney, who had made a secret personal €100,000 'bridging loan' to the FAI in 2017 that was hidden from the board, leading to his departure, Sport Ireland withholding funding, and comprehensive governance reforms of Irish soccer administration.

laws.title: Urban Regeneration and Development
laws.subtitle: Urban Regeneration and Housing Act 2015
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's urban regeneration policy targets derelict and vacant properties. The Derelict Sites Act 1990 allows local authorities to compulsorily acquire derelict properties, but enforcement has been weak. The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant (2022) provides up to €50,000 for renovating vacant or derelict properties. The Croí Cónaithe scheme supports urban apartment development. The Land Development Agency (LDA) develops state-owned land for housing. The 2023 Residential Zoned Land Tax targets landowners with rezoned but undeveloped sites. Heritage building conversion grants incentivize bringing older stock back to residential use.
laws.penalty: Failure to develop land subject to Residential Zoned Land Tax: annual tax of 3% of market value. Derelict Sites Levy: 7% of market value annually.
exceptions: Landowners with planning permission granted within timeframes exempt from RZLT
Protected structures have different development obligations

quiz.q: What annual tax targets owners of residentially zoned but undeveloped land in Ireland?
options: Residential Zoned Land Tax (3% of market value)
quiz.explanation: The Residential Zoned Land Tax (RZLT), introduced in 2022-2023, charges an annual tax of 3% of market value on land zoned for residential development that has not been built upon, aiming to incentivize landowners to develop or sell their land to address Ireland's housing shortage.

laws.title: Extradition and Mutual Legal Assistance
laws.subtitle: Extradition Acts 1965-2012 and EU Arrest Warrant Act 2003
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's extradition framework operates through the European Arrest Warrant (EAW) for EU states and bilateral treaties for non-EU countries. The Irish High Court reviews EAWs for compliance with fundamental rights and double criminality. High-profile cases: the lengthy extradition battles involving republican suspects during The Troubles created legal complexity. The Kinahan cartel's Liam Byrne had EAW proceedings. Jonathan Dowdall (politician who pleaded guilty to manslaughter) cooperated in the Hutch trial. UK-Ireland extradition under post-Brexit bilateral arrangements replaced EAW for UK.
laws.penalty: Resisting lawful extradition: contempt of court. EAW non-compliance: automatic enforcement by High Court.
exceptions: EAWs can be refused if fundamental rights would be violated
Political offense exception applies to non-EU extradition (though narrowed significantly)

quiz.q: What replaced the European Arrest Warrant for extradition between Ireland and the UK after Brexit?
quiz.explanation: After Brexit, the UK left the European Arrest Warrant system. Ireland and the UK now operate extradition through a bilateral arrangement agreed in the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement, which provides a similar but slightly different framework to the EAW for mutual extradition of suspects.

laws.title: Roma Rights and Anti-Discrimination
laws.subtitle: Equal Status Acts and Racial Equality Directive
laws.fullDescription: Roma EU citizens in Ireland face significant discrimination in housing, employment, education, and access to services. The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission (IHREC) has documented Roma as the most discriminated-against group in Ireland. Roma children face higher rates of school segregation and lower educational attainment. The Supreme Court's Pavee Point cases have clarified that Roma/Traveller ethnicity is a protected characteristic. Ireland's National Traveller and Roma Inclusion Strategy (2017-2021, updated 2022+) provides policy framework. Language barriers complicate service access for Roma who may not speak English or Irish.
laws.penalty: Discrimination against Roma on racial grounds: Equal Status Act complaint to WRC, compensation up to €15,000.
exceptions: Positive action measures targeting Roma/Traveller disadvantage are permitted
laws.sourceLabel: Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission

quiz.q: Which group has been identified as the most discriminated-against in Ireland according to IHREC documentation?
quiz.explanation: The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission (IHREC) has documented Roma as experiencing the highest rates of discrimination in Ireland, particularly in housing, employment, and education, despite Roma EU citizens having the same legal rights as other EU nationals.

laws.title: National Parks and Protected Areas
laws.subtitle: Wildlife Acts and National Parks Policy
laws.fullDescription: Ireland has six national parks (Wicklow Mountains, Killarney, Connemara, Glenveagh, Burren, Ballycroy) covering approximately 1% of the land area—among the lowest in Europe. The Natura 2000 network of SACs (Special Areas of Conservation) and SPAs (Special Protection Areas) covers much more. The government's 30x30 commitment (30% of land protected by 2030) will require significant expansion. Rewilding projects—restoring peat bogs, native woodland, and species—have gained momentum. The reintroduction of white-tailed eagles and red kite has been successful. Wolf reintroduction is being debated.
laws.penalty: Damage to SAC or SPA habitats: criminal prosecution and restoration orders, fines up to €250,000.
exceptions: Traditional agricultural activities in designated areas have management plan protections
Archaeological and heritage access permitted in national parks

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Ireland's land area is covered by national parks?
quiz.explanation: Ireland's six national parks cover approximately 1% of the country's land area, one of the lowest national park coverage rates in Europe. The government's 30x30 commitment (protecting 30% of land and sea by 2030) would require dramatic expansion of protected areas.

laws.title: Tax Evasion and Revenue Law
laws.subtitle: Taxes Consolidation Act 1997 — Criminal Provisions
laws.fullDescription: Revenue Commissioners have extensive audit and investigation powers. High-profile Irish tax evasion cases include the Ansbacher Account holders (offshore accounts in the Cayman Islands, 1990s), DIRT (Deposit Interest Retention Tax) evasion by banks, and the Tribunals of Inquiry (Flood/Mahon Tribunal on planning corruption, Moriarty Tribunal on politician payments). The 2023 Corporate Tax Roadmap addressed concerns about Ireland's global tax role. Revenue's Online Tax Compliance system processes €80+ billion annually. Voluntary disclosure facility allows pre-investigation settlement.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: up to 5 years imprisonment, 100% surcharge on evaded tax plus interest. PAYE fraud: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Innocent errors corrected by voluntary disclosure have reduced penalties
Small businesses below VAT thresholds have simplified compliance

quiz.q: What offshore account scandal involving Irish tax evasion in the Cayman Islands was exposed in the 1990s?
quiz.explanation: The Ansbacher Accounts scandal exposed how wealthy Irish businesspeople and others had secretly maintained offshore accounts in the Cayman Islands (held by Ansbacher Cayman Limited), evading Irish tax. The resulting investigation uncovered widespread tax evasion and links to political corruption.

laws.title: Social Enterprise and Credit Union Law
laws.subtitle: Credit Union Act 1997 and Social Enterprise Policy
laws.fullDescription: Irish credit unions are significant financial institutions serving 3.5 million members (about 75% of adults) and holding €18 billion in assets. The Credit Union Act 1997 and subsequent reforms (Credit Union and Co-operation with Overseas Regulators Act 2012) govern this sector. The Central Bank of Ireland regulates credit unions. Irish credit unions have been slower to expand their loan products compared to international counterparts. Social enterprises (community businesses with social objectives) are growing but lack dedicated legislation—operating under company law with social purpose. The Social Enterprise Policy (2019-2022) provided €5 million in annual support.
laws.penalty: Credit union regulatory violations: Central Bank enforcement, fines, and ultimately license revocation.
exceptions: Community credit unions with assets under €100 million have proportionate regulatory requirements
Voluntary credit unions with limited commercial activity have simplified rules

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Irish adults are members of a credit union?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 75% of Irish adults are members of a credit union, one of the highest credit union membership rates in the world, reflecting the deep roots of the cooperative financial model in Irish communities since the early 20th century.

laws.title: Homelessness Law and Right to Housing
laws.subtitle: Housing Acts and Homelessness Policy
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's constitution does not explicitly guarantee a right to housing, though the courts have interpreted related rights. Approximately 13,000 people were in emergency accommodation in 2023—the highest recorded. The Housing First model (permanent housing with support) has been expanded. Rough sleepers are a visible crisis in Dublin. Local authorities have legal obligations to provide emergency accommodation but capacity is chronically insufficient. The 2024 referendum on adding housing rights to the constitution was passed (March 2024)—inserting an obligation on the state to provide housing within available resources.
laws.penalty: Local authority failure to provide emergency accommodation: legal challenge, though enforcement is weak.
exceptions: International protection applicants (asylum seekers) have separate IPAS accommodation system
Domestic violence victims have priority pathway in emergency accommodation

quiz.q: What did Ireland's 2024 housing referendum achieve?
options: Inserted state obligation to provide housing into the constitution
Created a constitutional right to free housing
Required government to build 50,000 homes per year
quiz.explanation: Ireland's March 2024 housing referendum (the Fortieth Amendment) inserted a provision into the Constitution placing an obligation on the state to provide housing within available resources, stopping short of an absolute right to housing but establishing constitutional recognition of the housing crisis.

laws.title: Obscenity and Censorship
laws.subtitle: Censorship of Publications Acts 1929-1967
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's 1929 Censorship of Publications Act created a Censorship Board that banned thousands of books—notoriously including works by Samuel Beckett, Seán O'Casey, John McGahern, John Banville, and most major Irish authors. The 1967 Act limited bans to 12 years. Most bans lapsed by 1980s. Film censorship under the Official Film Censor was more persistent—director of film classification now. No books are currently banned for literary content. The blasphemy provision was removed (2018). Child pornography is criminalized under Child Trafficking and Pornography Act 1998 (and not subject to censorship debates).
laws.penalty: Child pornography possession: up to 5 years imprisonment. Distribution: up to 14 years.
exceptions: Legitimate literary, academic, and artistic works expressly protected from censorship
Film classification system rates but does not ban films (except for most extreme material)

quiz.q: What did Ireland's 1967 amendment to the Censorship of Publications Act change?
options: Limited book bans to a maximum of 12 years
quiz.explanation: The 1967 amendment to Ireland's Censorship of Publications Act limited all future book bans to a maximum of 12 years, after which they would automatically lapse. This led to most famous banned works—including those of Beckett, O'Casey, and other major Irish authors—becoming legally available.

laws.title: Just Transition and Peat Bogs
laws.subtitle: Just Transition Fund and Climate Action Plan
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's midlands relied heavily on peat (turf) harvesting for electricity generation and domestic heating. Bord na Móna operated vast peat bogs and power stations until 2020 when commercial peat harvesting largely ended. The Just Transition Fund (€11 million from 2020, expanding) supports midlands communities affected by the transition away from peat. Peatland restoration (by raising water tables) is a major carbon sequestration opportunity—Irish peatlands could store carbon equivalent to removing millions of cars. Domestic turf cutting for home heating remains a deeply cultural practice and political flashpoint.
laws.penalty: Industrial peat extraction without license: EPA enforcement. Unauthorized turf cutting in protected blanket bogs: NPWS enforcement actions.
exceptions: Domestic turf cutting on private unprotected bogs is legal
Traditional turf rights on commonage land maintained for local communities

quiz.q: What happened to commercial peat harvesting in Ireland in 2020?
options: Bord na Móna ended commercial peat harvesting for electricity generation
Peat harvesting was banned entirely including for domestic use
quiz.explanation: In 2020, Bord na Móna largely ended commercial peat harvesting for electricity generation, transitioning its operations toward renewable energy and peatland restoration. The Edenderry power station converted from peat to biomass, marking the end of Ireland's century-long reliance on peat-fired electricity generation.

laws.title: Brexit and Irish Border Impact
laws.subtitle: Northern Ireland Protocol and Windsor Framework
laws.fullDescription: Brexit had profound implications for Ireland as the only EU member state sharing a land border with the UK. The Irish government negotiated hard to protect the Good Friday Agreement and avoid a hard border. The Northern Ireland Protocol (2020) kept Northern Ireland in the EU Single Market for goods, creating a de facto border in the Irish Sea for some trade—causing political controversy in Northern Ireland (DUP opposition, loyalist protests). The Windsor Framework (2023) refined arrangements. The Common Travel Area preserved free movement for Irish and British citizens. Ireland became the EU's gateway to the UK in some respects.
laws.penalty: No domestic criminal penalties; border arrangements enforced through EU customs law and UK border procedures.
exceptions: Personal travel and movement of people between Ireland and UK unaffected (CTA)
Small businesses below trade thresholds have simplified procedures

quiz.q: What arrangement in the Brexit deal kept Northern Ireland effectively in the EU Single Market for goods?
quiz.explanation: The Northern Ireland Protocol (later modified by the Windsor Framework in 2023) kept Northern Ireland in the EU's Single Market for goods while the rest of the UK left, creating different customs arrangements between Great Britain and Northern Ireland and avoiding a hard land border on the island of Ireland.

laws.title: Education Law and School Patronage
laws.subtitle: Education Acts 1998-2018
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's school system is unusual: approximately 90% of state-funded schools are under Catholic Church patronage. The state funds schools but typically doesn't own them—the Church provides the buildings. The Education Act 1998 enshrined parental choice and school autonomy. The 2018 Education (Admission to Schools) Act restricted schools from prioritizing children of past pupils and children based on religious beliefs in admissions (except for schools oversubscribed where religion is part of ethos). Educate Together (multi-denominational), An Chomhairle um Oideachas Gaeltachta agus Gaelscolaíochta (Irish-medium), and Community National Schools are non-Catholic patronage models.
laws.penalty: School admissions discrimination beyond permitted criteria: equality complaints and sanctions.
exceptions: Oversubscribed religious schools may give priority to members of religion when it is central to school ethos (limited exception)
Special schools for specific needs have different admission frameworks

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Irish state-funded schools are under Catholic Church patronage?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 90% of Irish state-funded primary schools are under Catholic Church patronage—an unusually high rate for a Western democracy. This means the Church controls the ethos and management of schools that are funded by the state and attended by all children, including those of other faiths.

laws.title: Medical Negligence Law
laws.subtitle: Civil Liability Acts and Medical Practitioners Act 2007
laws.fullDescription: Medical negligence in Ireland follows the Dunne v. National Maternity Hospital standard: a doctor is not negligent if acting in accordance with a responsible body of medical opinion. The Medical Council regulates doctors and can remove registration for serious misconduct. High-profile cases include the CervicalCheck scandal (2018): women were not informed that their smear tests had been reviewed and found abnormal after cancer diagnoses—224 affected women, leading to the Scally Report and enhanced patient rights. The Patient Safety (Notifiable Incidents and Open Disclosure) Act 2023 requires mandatory disclosure of serious patient safety events.
laws.penalty: Medical negligence: civil damages. Serious professional misconduct: Medical Council de-registration. Open disclosure failure: regulatory sanction.
exceptions: Risk of therapeutic privilege (non-disclosure of information causing patient harm) has been significantly restricted
Liability can be managed through Clinical Indemnity Scheme (state-funded)

quiz.q: What 2018 scandal involved women not being told their smear tests had been reviewed and found abnormal?
options: Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital inquiry
quiz.explanation: The CervicalCheck scandal (2018) emerged when Vicky Phelan's legal case revealed that 221 (later 224) women had not been informed that their cervical smear tests had been retrospectively reviewed and found to be abnormal after they were diagnosed with cancer, leading to the Scally Report and significant patient rights reforms.

laws.title: Broadcasting Law and RTÉ
laws.subtitle: Broadcasting Acts 2009 and 2022
laws.fullDescription: RTÉ (Radio Teilifís Éireann) is Ireland's national public broadcaster, funded by a combination of the TV license (€160/year), commercial advertising, and state grants. The TV license model has faced severe stress—collection rates are low and streaming households avoid it. The Future of Media Commission (2022) recommended direct state funding. RTÉ's 2023 Ryan Tubridy payment scandal led to mass resignations from its board and executive and emergency government intervention. TG4 (Irish language) receives separate direct state funding. Virgin Media Television and Newstalk/Today FM are commercial competitors.
laws.penalty: TV license evasion: fixed penalty of €200. Garda can prosecute persistent evaders.
exceptions: Over-70s receive free TV license (welfare provision)
Exemptions for certain disability and social welfare recipients

quiz.q: How much is the annual TV license fee in Ireland?
quiz.explanation: Ireland's TV license costs €160 per year and is legally required for any premises with a television set. The license funds RTÉ (public broadcaster), though collection rates are low and the model is under review following the Future of Media Commission recommendations.

laws.title: Judicial Appointments and Independence
laws.subtitle: Courts Acts and Judicial Appointments Commission Act 2023
laws.fullDescription: Irish judges are appointed by the President on the advice of the Government, which had traditionally led to political appointments. The 2023 Judicial Appointments Commission Act reformed the process, creating an independent Judicial Appointments Commission to recommend candidates, reducing (but not eliminating) political influence. The Supreme Court has 9 members including the Chief Justice. Ireland has a civil law system derived from common law with EU law overlay. Judges serve until age 70 (with limited exceptions). The judiciary has been notably independent—striking down laws, invalidating government actions, and protecting constitutional rights vigorously.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for judicial appointment processes; commission independence maintained through legislative safeguards.
exceptions: Appointment of Attorney General has separate constitutional procedure
Temporary judicial appointments for specific purposes may be expedited

quiz.q: What reform did Ireland's 2023 Judicial Appointments Commission Act make to judicial selection?
options: Created independent commission to recommend candidates, reducing political influence
Abolished government role in judicial appointments entirely
Required judicial elections by public vote
Extended mandatory retirement age from 65 to 70
quiz.explanation: The 2023 Judicial Appointments Commission Act created an independent Judicial Appointments Commission to assess candidates and recommend names for judicial appointment, reducing (though not eliminating) the traditional political influence in judicial selection that had drawn criticism for years.

laws.title: Pharmaceutical Liability and Drug Safety
laws.subtitle: Health Products Regulatory Authority Act and Medicinal Products Regulations
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's pharmaceutical manufacturing sector requires strict compliance with EMA (European Medicines Agency) standards. The HPRA (Health Products Regulatory Authority) licenses medicines for Irish market. Thalidomide caused birth defects in Ireland as elsewhere (1950s-60s); Irish survivors received state compensation in 2023 after decades of advocacy. The COVID-19 vaccine rollout was managed by HPRA under EMA emergency authorization. Medical device safety (following EU MDR 2017 implementation) is increasingly important given Ireland's large medical device manufacturing sector (Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Cook Medical).
laws.penalty: Supplying unlicensed medicines: up to 5 years imprisonment. Clinical trial violations: serious regulatory and criminal consequences.
exceptions: Named patient schemes allow access to unlicensed medicines for individual patients with no alternatives
Hospital exemption for pharmacy-prepared medicines

quiz.q: When did Ireland finally provide state compensation to thalidomide survivors?
quiz.explanation: Ireland provided state compensation to thalidomide survivors in 2023, following decades of advocacy. Irish thalidomide survivors had long campaigned for recognition and compensation, with Ireland being one of the last countries to provide formal state acknowledgment and financial redress.

laws.title: Transport Infrastructure Law
laws.subtitle: Roads Act 1993 and National Transport Authority Act 2008
laws.fullDescription: Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) manages motorways, national roads, and major infrastructure. The National Transport Authority (NTA) plans and funds public transport. BusConnects (Dublin bus network redesign), the MetroLink (Dublin underground, planning stage), and DART+ (electrified rail expansion) are major projects. Ireland's rail network (Iarnród Éireann) is relatively limited by European standards. The 2022 National Development Plan allocated €35 billion to transport. The planning system for major infrastructure projects has faced significant delays. Electric vehicle charging infrastructure is expanding under the Climate Action Plan.
laws.penalty: Obstruction of transport infrastructure works: court injunction and contempt proceedings.
exceptions: Protected structures along transport routes may require modified alignment
Agricultural access to land cut by new roads maintained under Roads Act

quiz.q: How much did Ireland's 2022 National Development Plan allocate to transport infrastructure?
quiz.explanation: Ireland's 2022 National Development Plan allocated €35 billion to transport infrastructure over the plan period, covering projects including BusConnects, the MetroLink Dublin underground, DART+ rail electrification, motorway maintenance, and cycling infrastructure.

laws.title: Coastal Communities and Rights of Way
laws.subtitle: Coastal Access Rights and Foreshore Act 1933
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's Foreshore Act 1933 governs the inter-tidal zone. Public access to beaches is technically via rights of way rather than a general coastal access right—unlike Scotland's Land Reform Act right to roam. The 2016 Land and Conveyancing Law Reform Act provided some clarification. Hundreds of unofficial coastal access routes have been closed by landowners. The 2023 Marine Protected Areas Act created new coastal protection obligations. Swimming safety (Blue Flag beaches) is managed by local authorities. Coastal erosion threatens communities—the Climate Change Advisory Council recommends managed retreat in some areas.
laws.penalty: Blocking established right of way: civil action for nuisance or trespass. Foreshore development without license: enforcement by Marine Survey Office.
exceptions: Traditional fishing rights over foreshore maintained in many areas
Emergency access for safety and coastguard operations
laws.sourceLabel: Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage

quiz.q: Unlike Scotland's right to roam, how do Irish people generally access beaches and coastal areas?
options: Via specific rights of way rather than a general access right
Through land owned by local authorities
Via mandatory public easements on all coastal land
Under constitutional right to coastal access
quiz.explanation: Unlike Scotland (which has a general right of responsible access to land and water under the Land Reform Act 2003), Ireland has no general coastal access right. People access beaches through specific rights of way, traditional routes, or land owned by local authorities, leaving many coastal paths vulnerable to closure by private landowners.

laws.title: Agricultural Crime and Rural Security
laws.subtitle: Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act and Garda Rural Community Support
laws.fullDescription: Agricultural crime is a significant concern in rural Ireland: theft of farm equipment, machinery, livestock, and diesel are major issues. The Garda Rural Community Support Office addresses rural crime specifically. Farm invasions and attacks on elderly rural residents have caused significant fear. Metal theft affecting agricultural infrastructure is prosecuted under the Scrap Metal Dealer Registration Act. The Rural Crime Action Plan (2022) includes dedicated Garda resources. Farmwatch—a community alert system—operates nationwide. Vehicle theft using relay attacks on keyless entry systems is a growing agricultural crime.
laws.penalty: Livestock theft: up to 10 years (same as general theft). Aggravated burglary at dwelling: up to life imprisonment.
exceptions: Estray livestock (animals straying onto roads) have civil law framework for resolution
Livestock seizures by enforcement bodies (DSP, courts) are not theft

quiz.q: What community alert system operates in rural Ireland to prevent agricultural crime?
quiz.explanation: Farmwatch is Ireland's community-based rural crime prevention alert system, allowing farmers and rural residents to share information about suspicious activity through a text and social media alert network, supported by An Garda Síochána's Rural Community Support Office.

laws.title: Intellectual Property Law
laws.subtitle: Copyright and Related Rights Act 2000
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's IP framework implements EU Directives and TRIPS Agreement. Copyright lasts 70 years post-mortem auctoris. Patents are registered through the Irish Patents Office (part of IPOI) or via European Patent Office. Trade mark registration is through IPOI or EUIPO. The Knowledge Development Box offers a reduced 6.25% corporation tax rate on income from patented inventions and certain copyrights. Ireland amended its copyright law for the EU Copyright Directive (2022) including press publishers' rights and value gap provisions for user-uploaded content. Pharmaceutical patent litigation is significant given the sector's importance.
laws.penalty: Copyright infringement: damages, injunctions, up to 5 years and €126,000 fine for commercial piracy. Patent infringement: commercial damages.
exceptions: Research exception for non-commercial scientific research
Quotation and criticism for review is permitted fair dealing

quiz.q: What tax rate does Ireland's Knowledge Development Box offer on income from patented inventions?
quiz.explanation: Ireland's Knowledge Development Box (KDB) offers a reduced corporation tax rate of 6.25% (half the standard 12.5% rate) on income derived from qualifying intellectual property, particularly patented inventions and certain copyrights from qualifying R&D activity, incentivizing IP-intensive business in Ireland.

laws.title: Peace and Reconciliation Policy
laws.subtitle: Reconciliation Fund and Shared Island Initiative
laws.fullDescription: Ireland's government has allocated significant resources to promoting reconciliation between communities divided by The Troubles. The Reconciliation Fund (Department of Foreign Affairs) supports cross-community initiatives on the island of Ireland. The Shared Island Initiative (2020), with €500 million in funding, promotes all-island cooperation in infrastructure, research, and culture. The Implementation Bodies of the Good Friday Agreement (Waterways Ireland, InterTradeIreland, Tourism Ireland, etc.) operate on a North-South basis. The 2023 Legacy Act (UK) created a Troubled Times unit but was opposed by Irish government and victims' groups.
laws.penalty: No domestic criminal penalties; the Shared Island and reconciliation frameworks are policy rather than criminal law.
exceptions: Legacy prosecutions for Troubles-era crimes remain contentious and subject to ongoing legal challenges
Conditional early release of Troubles prisoners under GFA was a one-time provision
laws.sourceLabel: Department of Foreign Affairs — Shared Island

quiz.q: How much funding did Ireland's 2020 Shared Island Initiative allocate for all-island cooperation?
quiz.explanation: Ireland's Shared Island Initiative, launched in 2020, allocated €500 million to promote all-island cooperation in infrastructure, research, tourism, education, and community relations, reflecting the Irish government's commitment to deepening practical cooperation on the island of Ireland within the framework of the Good Friday Agreement.
